strengths: MaskSub provides a simple, technically coherent way to use strong masking in supervised training: the masked pass learns from detached predictions of the unmasked pass while sharing parameters. It adds no inference overhead and works with existing training recipes. Its practical usefulness and substantial empirical support favor weak acceptance.

The main classification results are convincing. Table 1 reports improvements across ViT-S/B/L/H at both 400 and 800 epochs, including gains of 0.6–0.7 percentage points at 400 epochs. Selected results include uncertainty estimates: Table A.12 reports ViT-B improving from 83.46±0.04 to 84.08±0.02, supporting an effect beyond run variability.

The paper meaningfully accounts for additional computation. Table 7 shows ViT-B reaching 84.1% in 25 GPU days versus 83.7% for longer baseline training in 26 GPU days. Under the common recipe in Table 8, MaskSub also achieves higher accuracy than CoSub with lower measured cost: 84.1% at 25.1 GPU days versus 83.9% at 35.3.

Evaluation extends well beyond one architecture or classification setting. Results cover ResNet, Swin, several pretrained-model finetuning recipes, and downstream vision tasks. Table A.2 reports consistent ADE20K improvements, while Table A.4 shows gains across multiple distribution shifts, including ImageNet-A improving from 36.8% to 41.9% for ViT-B. These results strengthen the contribution to visual representation learning.

The supplementary material provides useful component evidence and implementation detail. Table A.6 shows that removing the distillation loss substantially reduces the improvement, and Tables A.7–A.8 examine masking ratios and loss weights. Algorithm 1, detailed training configurations, and repeated-run results for selected experiments make the central method reasonably reproducible.
weaknesses: The conceptual novelty is moderate: the method combines established asymmetric self-distillation with masked inputs and token removal. Its relationship to weak-to-strong prediction consistency deserves sharper treatment. Table A.7 already improves accuracy from 77.4% to 78.4% with zero masking, versus 79.2% with 50% masking, showing that part of the benefit comes from the general two-pass distillation procedure. The strongest contribution is the effective integration and validation, rather than a fundamentally new learning objective.

The explanation of automatic difficulty control overstates what is established. Section 3.1 says masking is effectively restricted to images producing successful predictions, but Eq. (3) trains every masked example against the current teacher prediction, including potentially confident errors. Figure 3 supports an aggregate change in gradient contributions, not correctness-based selection. Likewise, Figure 2 demonstrates faster convergence per epoch; it does not by itself establish faster convergence in wall-clock time.

Table 6 does not establish superiority over the listed historical self-distillation methods independently of training recipe differences. The accompanying inference that methods evaluated with weaker recipes are incompatible with stronger recipes is unsupported. The controlled comparisons with CoSub and GradAug are substantially more persuasive and should define the scope of comparative claims.

Claims of consistently significant improvement need qualification. Table 10 shows ViT-B CIFAR-100 accuracy falling from 91.7% to 89.6% when MaskSub is used in both pretraining and finetuning. Section 4.2 explicitly states that the best CLIP finetuning accuracy is unchanged, despite better final-epoch results. Although selected experiments include repeated runs, the 0.1-point BEiT-v2 gains and small detection improvements lack uncertainty estimates, limiting conclusions about those individual settings.

There are correctable numerical reporting errors. Table 10 labels the ViT-S Cars change from 80.9% to 92.2% as +1.3 rather than +11.3 points. Section 4.4 claims approximately one-sixth of GradAug's training cost, whereas Table 9 reports 8.6 versus 23.4 GPU days, approximately 37% of total cost. These require correction but do not negate the broader empirical contribution.
